title: Books & Language Shorts · Episode 2
chapters: What your eyes and brain do when you read

units.t: Books & Language Shorts. Episode two.
In this episode: What your eyes and brain do when you read and The hidden shapes of stories.
Part one. What your eyes and brain do when you read.
Reading feels smooth and effortless, but your eyes are jumping, stopping and skipping all the time.
And your brain is using circuits that evolved for something else.
A borrowed brain.
Humans have been speaking for at least tens of thousands of years, probably far longer, but writing was invented only around 5,000 years ago, and mass literacy is barely a few centuries old.
That is far too recent for evolution to have produced a brain built for reading.
The neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene proposed a theory called neuronal recycling.
Learning to read repurposes circuits that evolved for other jobs, such as recognising objects and faces, and links them to the brain's language areas.
In children learning to read, scans show a region on the underside of the left hemisphere becoming increasingly tuned to written letters and words.
It is often called the visual word form area.
Recognising words.
The visual word form area sits in the left fusiform gyrus, near areas that respond to faces and objects.
It helps us recognise a word whether it is written in capitals, lower case or different fonts, an impressive feat of pattern recognition.
Damage to this area, for example from a stroke, can cause a condition in which a person can still write but struggles to read back what they have just written.
Research also suggests that learning to read changes the brain in other ways, including how it processes spoken sounds.
This partly explains why reading and phonics are so closely linked.
Eyes jump, not glide.
Watch someone's eyes as they read and you will see they do not move smoothly along the line.
They make quick jumps called saccades, separated by brief pauses called fixations.
In English, a typical fixation lasts roughly a quarter of a second, and a typical jump covers around seven to nine letters.
During the jump itself, you take in almost no useful visual information.
The brain stitches the pauses together so that reading feels continuous.
Readers skip many short, predictable words, such as the and of, and land more often on longer content words.
About one jump in ten or so goes backwards as the reader checks something.
Researchers study all this with eye trackers, which record exactly where and when the eyes stop.
The window of attention.
Sharp vision covers only a tiny part of what your eyes see, so at each fixation you can identify only a handful of letters clearly.
Experiments in which on-screen text changes depending on where the reader is looking have measured this window.
For English readers it extends roughly three or four letters to the left of the fixation point and about fourteen or fifteen to the right, because that is where the next words are.
For readers of Hebrew, which runs right to left, the window is reversed.
Information at the edge of the window helps the brain plan the next jump and get a head start on the next word.
Reading, in short, is constant prediction.
Speed reading and myths.
Typical silent reading speeds for adults are roughly 200 to 300 words per minute.
A major 2016 review led by the eye-movement scientist Keith Rayner concluded that speed reading claims of thousands of words per minute do not hold up.
The limit is the brain's speed in recognising words and understanding language, not the eyes.
Pushing faster means comprehension drops.
Speed reading is essentially skimming: useful for finding information, not for deep understanding.
Faster reading comes mainly from reading more.
The scrambled-letters meme claims research at Cambridge shows letter order does not matter if the first and last letters are right.
Matt Davis, a Cambridge scientist, found no such study.
The text works partly because many words are short, function words are intact, and letters stay near their correct positions.
Jumbled text still slows readers down.
The key idea: Writing is too recent for evolution to have built a reading brain, so reading repurposes circuits that evolved for other tasks.
Part two. The hidden shapes of stories.
Is there really only a handful of plots in the world?
Writers and scientists have long tried to map the hidden structures beneath the stories we love.
Early maps of plot.
Think of almost any film you have enjoyed.
Someone wants something, obstacles appear, things get worse, then there is a turning point and a resolution.
It feels natural, but people have tried to describe the pattern for over two thousand years.
In his Poetics, in the 4th century BCE, Aristotle observed that a good tragedy has a beginning, a middle and an end, and its events follow from one another by necessity or probability.
A plot is a chain of causes, not a list of events.
In 1863 the German critic Gustav Freytag drew drama as a five-part pyramid: introduction, rising action, climax, falling action and catastrophe or resolution.
It fits tragedies like Hamlet well, but suits many modern stories less well.
The hero's journey.
In 1949 the American scholar Joseph Campbell published The Hero with a Thousand Faces.
Drawing on myths from many cultures, he argued that hero stories often follow a similar path, which he called the monomyth.
A hero leaves the ordinary world after a call to adventure, often helped by a mentor.
The hero crosses into an unfamiliar world, faces trials and a great ordeal, gains a reward or insight, and returns home transformed.
Campbell became enormously influential in Hollywood.
George Lucas has said his work shaped Star Wars, and screenwriters later popularised the pattern as a practical template.
Critics argue Campbell picked examples that fit and ignored many that do not, but the idea remains widely used.
Counting the plots.

In 2004 the British journalist Christopher Booker published The Seven Basic Plots, arguing that stories fall into types such as overcoming the monster, rags to riches, the quest, comedy, tragedy and rebirth.
Others propose anywhere from three to over thirty.
Jaws and David and Goliath really are both about overcoming a monster.
But critics say the categories are so broad that almost anything fits.
Kurt Vonnegut drew stories as lines on a graph, with good fortune up and bad fortune down.
In 2016 US researchers analysed the emotional words in over 1,000 works of fiction and reported six basic emotional arcs.
Like all such studies, it is open to debate.
Other storytelling traditions.
Most of these models come from European and American traditions and assume stories are driven by conflict between a hero and an obstacle.
Other traditions work differently.

A classical structure from Chinese poetry, later used in Japanese and Korean storytelling and often called kishotenketsu in Japanese, has four parts: introduction, development, a twist and a conclusion that brings the parts together.
The twist need not be a conflict, just a surprising new angle.
Aboriginal storytelling traditions are often closely tied to land and place, and many stories connect to particular sites and to responsibilities for Country, rather than following one hero's arc.
These differences remind us that the Western plot is one model among many.
Why structure matters.
Knowing these patterns does not mean every story must follow them.
Many great books play with structure: they start at the end, tell events out of order, or refuse a tidy resolution.
But understanding the common shapes is useful.
As a reader, it helps you notice why a story feels satisfying or why it drags.
As a writer, it gives you questions to ask: what does the main character want, what stands in the way, and what changes by the end?
Psychologists have also found that people tend to remember information better when it is told as a story with causes and consequences.
That may be why the same shapes keep appearing, from campfire tales to streaming series.
We seem to think in stories.
The key idea: Thinkers from Aristotle to Freytag described plot as a chain of causes that rises and falls.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. How does the brain manage to read despite writing being so recent?
Answer. It repurposes circuits from other tasks.
Question two. What was Aristotle's key point about plot?
Answer. Events should follow from one another as a chain of causes.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
